not specified teku does, but theres no requirement OK, what about Prysm <@755590043632140352> ? also though as a solo staker you'd be unlikely to be proposing in a realistic timeframe for that to be important if you're someone like lido, then yes, the numbers are different 🙂 maybe a bad example... allnodes, or one of the institutionals they propose often enough that local selection is advantageous No, we do LIFO, there's no more security to hacked keys prioritizing The pre submitted keys and it incentivizes flooding the fork The only advantage of submitting pre fork is that they will be broadcasted earlier we've seen something like ahm...36k BLS changes on goerli already just for context... if your keys are safe, wait a while - even a few days, and there wont' be a queue to speak of, and it'll be really simple the eth isn't going anywhere until you make the change, so its really an 'at your leisure' scenario imo lodestar can also convert it to LIFO except if you need ot cash out or your keys are compromised, then im sure there's reasons if thats recommended no its fine, leave it I know, this is purely because I had a discussion with <@453386940490711054> yesterday about CLWP and me not being entirely sure about client behavior Thanks for clarifying guys 🙂 any time! the real question is if you're comfortable your keys are safe, and i cant answer that one but if you need to talk things through there's defintiely people that can listen and give their 2c if you need more info I'm OK myself, but have assisted/explained consequences to quite a few that lost sole-ownership of their mnemonic... There's definitely people they should be talking to, sounds like you're across all that 🙂 Things that matter: - getting in to your local beacon node's list of pending withdrawals (this stops an attacker from providing their own change operation) - having your operation broadcast to other nodes (this stops an attacker from propagating their own change operation) Things that don't matter: - when the operation is included on-chain (at least, no one will care in a month) IMO noone will care in a matter of days... the queue will clear so fast it'll make peoples heads spin... after the initial push the queue will practically always be empty unless an institutional pushes a large batch thats why if your keys are secure, just chilling is probably easiest answer oh and making sure your clients are updated, as evidence today 🙂 I know myself will take several days to actually prepare the signed messages 🙂 I think this is probably the best way to convey the message I'm not sure how we can clearly articulate this to a "general" audience without it being overly confusing to the average staker 😅 - send your credentials change operation as soon as you are comfortable to do so - don't worry if it takes a while to take effect The thing is, if you look at beaconchain and there's a large queue, I'd hold off, or you'l be waiting for a while before you can see that it worked. For me, I like to do things that i can check worked, then never think about it again, so if i change BLS creds and can check in 15 minutes and see it's complete, that'd be ideal.... I'd probably be obsessively checking every 12 minutes for a day if i did it when there's a queue of 35000 like yesterday More of a reason, I think after a couple of epochs, a user that submits will be able to check the change on-chain in just 2-3 blocks max he needs to be very unlucky of grabbing a pool sending all their fleet at the same time, right after him Maybe - Check if you even need to change your credentials - if you setup your validator with an ethereum withdrawal address, then this is not a process that will involve you... - If you do need to change your credentials, and you have no concerns for the security of your withdrawal mnemonic, then change it any time after capella, and there's no rush. Find a time that best suits you when you're not distracted and can spend a little time reading some documentation, You'll need an ethereum address that you can deposit funds to and definitely have control of... Make sure you still have the credentials for the ethereum address you're going to use, as the change is permanent for the validator.... etc .etc. There's definitely the number of bls changes on the withdrawals page, but I suspect the size of the bls change queue is a little less easy to see... and querying the api isn't something I'd probably suggest non tech users play with as they'll just find it frustrating, so that's the part of the story im not sure how to articulate in a way that everyone will get and be appropriate for their client... currently there's 318 437 BLS withdrawal keys on mainnet, and 232 596 eth withdrawal addresses, if it helps frame the discussion... Maybe
 - Check if you even need to change your credentials - if you setup your validator with an ethereum withdrawal address, then this is not a process that will involve you...
 - If you do need to change your credentials, and you have no concerns for the security of your withdrawal mnemonic, then change it any time after capella, and there's no rush.
